domain: International Law / Political Philosophy / International Relations
topic_summary: Analysis of the Westphalian sovereignty doctrine as a contested kernel in international law, examining the collision between traditional absolutist readings (domestic jurisdiction as inviolable) and conditional readings through the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) framework. The contest determines the legal and epistemic boundaries of legitimate international coercion.

key_entities: Westphalian State (territorial sovereign claiming absolute domestic jurisdiction)
UN Security Council (institutional authority structure for R2P invocations)
Humanitarian intervention coalitions (ad hoc enforcement outside UNSC)
Domestic populations (victim set varies by reading)
key_tensions: Absolute sovereignty vs conditional sovereignty (kernel contest)
UNSC monopoly vs unilateral intervention (authority structure)
key_mechanisms: UNSC Chapter VII authorization (formal R2P pathway)
State practice as customary law formation (kernel drift mechanism)
key_absences: Economic sovereignty (trade/finance coercion not addressed in R2P framework)
Colonial legacy influence on which states face R2P scrutiny
Threshold measurement for 'mass atrocity' trigger (epistemic ambiguity)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The Westphalian sovereignty doctrine as foundational practice-norm stabilizing territorial state's claim to non-interference in domestic affairs
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: UN Charter Article 2(7) as textual anchor; UNSC as interpretive authority with veto structure preserving great power privilege; ICJ as secondary interpretive body; state practice as customary law formation mechanism
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: Ambiguity Exploitation Pattern (AEP) — the kernel's deliberate vagueness about sovereignty's limits allows selective interpretation by UNSC permanent members; R2P as formalized interpretive layer absorbing humanitarian norm drift without revising Charter text

readings.commitment: Sovereignty grants inviolable domestic jurisdiction; external intervention is categorically impermissible regardless of internal conduct
readings.authority_grounding: UN Charter Article 2(7) literal text; Treaty of Westphalia (1648) as historical foundation; state practice norm of non-interference
readings.expected_structural_delta: All domestic populations outside victim set for international law purposes; domestic regime is sole rights-holder; zero legitimate external coercion threshold; high suppression of humanitarian intervention norm

readings.commitment: Sovereignty is conditional on state protecting populations from mass atrocities; failure triggers residual international responsibility
readings.authority_grounding: 2005 World Summit Outcome Document; UNSC resolutions 1674, 1973; 'sovereignty as responsibility' doctrine (Deng/ICISS)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Populations suffering mass atrocities enter victim set; international community becomes residual rights-holder; UNSC becomes constraint arbiter; moderate suppression of unilateral intervention but licensed multilateral coercion

readings.commitment: Sovereignty is spectrum of legitimacy correlating with domestic governance quality; intervention legitimacy scales with regime type and conduct severity
readings.authority_grounding: Democratic peace theory; 'illegal but legitimate' intervention doctrine (Kosovo 1999); emerging norm of democratic sovereignty
readings.expected_structural_delta: Victim set determined by governance-quality threshold (authoritarian regimes more vulnerable); legitimacy decoupled from legality; coalitions of democracies as de facto arbiter; minimal suppression of unilateral intervention by 'legitimate' actors

axiom_contradictions.basis: Absolutist treats sovereignty as categorical right independent of internal conduct; R2P treats sovereignty as conditional status dependent on performance. No single framework can hold both: either sovereignty is categorically inviolable or it is not.

Absolutist treats all states as equal holders of sovereignty regardless of regime type; gradated treats sovereignty as legitimacy spectrum varying by governance quality. No framework can hold both: either sovereignty is regime-neutral or it is regime-dependent.

omegas.description: Are these three genuinely distinct readings or merely tactical invocations of one malleable kernel? If all states cite whichever reading suits immediate interests, the kernel may not be contested but deliberately indeterminate (pure AEP). Empirical test: do states maintain reading consistency across cases or switch opportunistically?

Absolutist and R2P readings coexist as socially live positions (coexists_with edge) yet hold axiom-contradictory foundations. This identifies licensed plurality: the system permits both to operate because ambiguity serves the UNSC permanent members. Is this stable or degrading toward one reading's dominance?

Economic coercion (sanctions, structural adjustment) excluded from R2P framework despite causing humanitarian crises comparable to those triggering military intervention. Is this exclusion sustainable as debt-trap diplomacy and financial warfare proliferate? Deferred axis may warrant generation if focus expands beyond military intervention.

omegas.description: R2P lacks operational atrocity threshold. Is this epistemic gap or deliberate ambiguity (AEP feature)? If the former, legal scholarship should converge on metric; if latter, discretion is the point. Deferred axis suggests latter but requires institutional analysis.

omegas.description: Does sovereignty doctrine extend to cyberspace? State practice emerging around 'digital sovereignty' may instantiate fourth reading of kernel or constitute separate kernel entirely. Not addressed in extraction but structurally adjacent.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel recognition supported by: (1) shared substrate (sovereignty doctrine) all parties argue about, (2) readings emit structurally different constraints (victim sets, enforcement mechanisms, suppression levels differ), (3) axiom contradictions confirmed for absolutist vs R2P and absolutist vs gradated pairs. Licensed plurality pattern (axiom-contradictory yet socially coexistent readings) documented in omega_licensed_plurality.
